title: It's Not About Freedom
author: Peter Greene
summary: School choice vouchers are not about empowering parents or unleashing parental rights, but about abandoning collective responsibility for education. Vouchers reframe education as an individual problem rather than a societal investment, telling families their child's education is now solely their responsibility. The rhetoric of freedom masks policies of abandonment that benefit those already advantaged while withdrawing support from everyone else. True freedom requires not just individual choice but the resources and structures that make meaningful choice possible for all.
points: Voucher programs prioritize private school rights over families' ability to choose, allowing schools to exclude, charge extra, and operate without accountability.
School choice rhetoric masks policies of abandonment, reframing education from collective responsibility to individual problem.
Vouchers guarantee less purchasing power than public systems, forcing families to supplement costs while losing the benefit of pooled resources.
The freedom advocates celebrate is actually freedom from responsibility for others, not freedom for the disadvantaged.
Without equitable access to resources, adequate funding, and information, school choice becomes a system where advantaged families thrive and vulnerable ones are abandoned.
quotes: Vouchers are about getting the government out of the education business and, by doing so, also get government out of the work of equity. Vouchers are about telling every family, Your kid's education is now your problem, and nobody else's. Society has washed its hands of you. Good luck.
Taxpayer-funded school choice vouchers are not about empowering parents or unleashing parental rights.
The idea simmering under school choice and now bubbling up all around us is simple, Why should I have to help take care of other people.
Freedom is a pretty word for dressing policies of abandonment.
The freedom being advocated for is freedom for me or freedom for those who deserve it. Or maybe freedom from worrying about anyone else.” Archived from Curmudgucation on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
